entries.name: eq_byte_constant_vs_concrete-accept#0
entries.script: [Q1] **CONTROL:** a specialised `Coll[Byte]` CONSTANT `==` a `ConcreteCollection` of the same three bytes is **`true`** at cost 58. Equality is NOT provenance-sensitive, so an implementation that models the two shapes must still compare them equal. Without this row the family could be 'passed' by making the shapes unequal.

entries.name: eq_bool_constant_vs_concrete-accept#1
entries.script: [Q2] **CONTROL:** the same on the `$mcZ$sp` kind, `true` at cost 58.

entries.name: eq_indices_vs_concrete-accept#2
entries.script: [Q3] **CONTROL:** `indices` (`$mcI$sp`) `==` a ConcreteCollection of the same ints, `true` at cost 84.

entries.name: indexof_indices_cross_width-accept#3
entries.script: [X1] `indices.indexOf(x, 0)` where `x` is declared Int and evaluates to `1L`: **finds it at index 1**, cost 96 — the same answer as the well-typed control. `indexOf` is NOT defined on `CollOverArray`: `Colls.scala:199` is a trait default, `indexWhere(x => elem == x)`, so the item is compared with boxed `==` (numerically, across widths) and never cast. **CONTROL for the whole round:** a specialised receiver does NOT make every ill-typed argument fatal, and the rule is which methods the specialised class overrides.

entries.name: indexof_int_concrete_cross_width-accept#4
entries.script: [X2] The generic twin answers identically, `1` at cost 100. No separation, by design of the trait default.
